lesson.title: Any Exponent You Like: Generalizing the Power Rule
lesson.summary: Logarithmic differentiation proves that the power rule d/dx[f(x)^n] = n f(x)^(n-1) f'(x) holds for every real exponent n, not just the whole numbers and simple fractions covered by earlier methods.
lesson.body:
The basic power rule d/dx[x^n] = n x^(n-1) is usually proved first for positive whole numbers, then stretched to negative integers and rational exponents using the quotient rule and implicit differentiation. But what about an exponent like pi, or a case where the base is a whole expression rather than plain x? Logarithmic differentiation settles all of these questions at once, with a single short argument.

Let y = [f(x)]^n, where n is any fixed real number and f(x) > 0. Step one: ln y = n ln f(x), using the power law of logs. Step two: differentiating gives y'/y = n times f'(x)/f(x). Step three and four: solving for y' and substituting gives y' = y times n f'(x)/f(x) = [f(x)]^n times n f'(x)/f(x) = n [f(x)]^(n-1) f'(x), where the last simplification just uses the exponent law [f(x)]^n / f(x) = [f(x)]^(n-1). This is the general power rule, and it now covers any real exponent n at all, matching the pattern already familiar from chain rule problems.

As a worked example, differentiate y = (x^2+4x+1)^(7/3). Here f(x) = x^2+4x+1 and n = 7/3. By the rule just derived, y' = (7/3)(x^2+4x+1)^(7/3 - 1) times (2x+4) = (7/3)(x^2+4x+1)^(4/3)(2x+4). This same answer could be found more quickly by treating it as an ordinary chain rule problem, outer power rule times inner derivative, and that shortcut is exactly what the log differentiation argument above justifies, even though 7/3 is not an integer.

Every example so far still has a fixed, constant exponent; only the base has been complicated. The next chapter removes that last restriction and asks what happens when the exponent itself changes with x, as in x^x, where log differentiation stops being a convenience and becomes the only clean way through.
